Rent Veil
RENT VAYL
n. (typological event)
From Old English rendan (to tear, rend; past tense rent) and Old French voile (veil, curtain; from Latin velum, a covering). “Rent” is the Authorised Version's past tense of “rend,” used of the temple curtain torn at the moment of Christ's death (Matt 27:51; Mark 15:38). The veil itself was the massive curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place in the Jerusalem Temple.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The rent veil is the dramatic and theologically decisive event recorded in all three Synoptic Gospels at the moment of Christ's death: the great curtain of the Temple separating the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies was torn in two from top to bottom. Matthew records: “Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matt 27:51). The direction of the tearing — from top to bottom — signals that the act was divine, not human: no human could have reached to tear from the ceiling downward. The veil itself was, according to Josephus, roughly four inches thick and so massive it required teams of men to hang it. That it was torn at the exact moment of Christ's expiration was not coincidence but covenant: His death was the event that abolished the old-covenant separation between God and His people. Hebrews 9:3 identifies the structure: “And behind the second veil there was a tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies.” Under the old covenant only the high priest could enter this space, and only once a year, never without blood. Christ's death changes everything: “Since we have confidence to enter the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which He inaugurated for us through the veil — that is, His flesh” (Heb 10:19–20). The rent veil is the spatial enactment of what the cross accomplishes: total, permanent, personal access for every believer to the presence of the living God, purchased by the blood of the Son whose body was itself the true veil.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a veil as a covering or curtain used to conceal or separate; in the temple context, the rent veil is the abolition of that separation between God and man at the moment of Christ's atoning death — the architectural announcement that the barrier of sin has been removed and the way into the Holy of Holies stands open for all who come by the blood of Jesus.

expand to see more

VEIL, n. [Fr. voile, L. velum.] A covering; something spread over or before a thing to conceal it. Webster (1828) notes the veil's use as a symbol of concealment and sacred separation — that which hides what is too holy or too dangerous for common approach. Moses veiled his face; the temple veil concealed the divine Presence.

RENT, pp. of REND. Torn; split asunder. Webster (1828): to rend is to tear with force — a violent, sudden separation. The temple veil was not opened, unlocked, or drawn back; it was rent — violently torn from above, signalling the violent, substitutionary tearing of Christ's flesh on the cross as the means by which the separation was abolished.

Key Scripture

Matthew 27:51 — "And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. And the earth shook — and the rocks were split."

Hebrews 10:19 — "Therefore, brothers — since we have confidence to enter the holy place by the blood of Jesus,"

Hebrews 10:20 — "by a new and living way which He inaugurated for us through the veil — that is, His flesh —"

Hebrews 9:3 — "And behind the second veil there was a tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies —"

Modern Corruption

Sacramentalism and sacerdotalism attempt to re-hang the veil by interposing a human priesthood between the believer and God; liberal scholarship treats the rent veil as Markan theology rather than historical event; and modern evangelicalism trivialises the access the rent veil represents by reducing prayer to casual conversation with a domesticated deity.

expand to see more

Roman Catholic and High Church Anglican sacramentalism effectively re-erects the veil by positioning an ordained priesthood as the indispensable mediator between the believer and the divine Presence. The Mass re-presents the sacrifice; the priest alone consecrates; the laity access God through the clerical office rather than directly through the torn veil of Christ's flesh. The book of Hebrews is a sustained polemic against this: Christ is the One High Priest who by a single offering “perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Heb 10:14). The rent veil means there is no need for another priest, another sacrifice, or another mediating office. The way in is open; every believer can enter the Holy of Holies with confidence.

Liberal historical critics routinely treat the rent veil as Markan theological symbolism retroactively inserted into the passion narrative — a literary device expressing the Gentile mission rather than a physical event. This move is standard historical-critical procedure: allegorize what is supernatural, historicize what is theological. The Synoptic unanimity — Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record the tearing — and the precise specification (“from top to bottom”) argue for a remembered event, not a retrofitted symbol. The theological meaning does not require the physical fact to be fictional; the fact is precisely the kind of providential sign God routinely sends alongside redemptive events.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The rent veil completes the entire tabernacle and temple system of Scripture: the Holy of Holies was God's symbolic dwelling-place on earth, the veil was the barrier of holiness that kept fallen humanity out, and Christ's death tore that barrier away — making every subsequent temple the body of each believer in whom the Spirit dwells.

expand to see more

Exodus 26:31–33 — God commands Moses to make the original tabernacle veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn with cherubim; it was hung before the Ark of the Covenant as the boundary of the divine Presence.

Leviticus 16 — the Day of Atonement ritual: the high priest enters behind the veil once per year with blood, making atonement for Israel's sins; the pattern fulfilled by Christ (Heb 9:11–12).

Hebrew pārôket — the inner veil of the tabernacle/temple, separating the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies; its name may derive from a root meaning “to separate.”

Greek katapetasma — the veil of the temple; the word used in Matt 27:51, Mark 15:38, Luke 23:45, and Hebrews 6:19; 9:3; 10:20.

Hebrews 10:20 — “through the veil — that is, His flesh”: Christ's body is identified as the true veil, making the literal tearing of the temple curtain a sacramental sign of the tearing of His incarnate flesh on the cross.

Usage

"The direction of the tearing — from top to bottom — is exegetically significant: the rent veil was not torn by grieving disciples from below but by God from above, declaring by a divine act that the separation His holiness required had been resolved by His Son's substitutionary death."

"Hebrews 10:19–22 turns the rent veil into a pastoral summons: “since we have confidence to enter the holy place by the blood of Jesus … let us draw near.” The theological reality demands a devotional response — believers are not to stand at the threshold but to enter, with full assurance of faith, into the presence of the living God."

"The identification of Christ's flesh as the true veil (Heb 10:20) means that the Incarnation is not only the mode of His humiliation but the structural reality His death tears open: the human nature He assumed became the “curtain” through which humanity gains access to God — and His crucifixion tore that curtain so that access is permanent and unimpeded."
